claim: Rhythmic cortical activity tracked the hierarchical rhythmic structures in audiovisually congruent human walking movements and footstep sounds.
source: Using electroencephalogram (EEG), we demonstrated that rhythmic cortical activity tracked the hierarchical rhythmic structures in audiovisually congruent human walking movements and footstep sounds.
evidence: The abstract states this as a demonstrated finding from EEG recordings.

claim: Cortical tracking effects exhibit an additive mode in a lower-order, narrower temporal integration window (step cycle).
source: Remarkably, the cortical tracking effects exhibit distinct multisensory integration modes at two temporal scales: an additive mode in a lower-order, narrower temporal integration window (step cycle) and a super-additive enhancement in a higher-order, broader temporal window (gait cycle).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about integration modes at different temporal scales.

claim: Cortical tracking effects exhibit a super-additive enhancement in a higher-order, broader temporal window (gait cycle).
source: Remarkably, the cortical tracking effects exhibit distinct multisensory integration modes at two temporal scales: an additive mode in a lower-order, narrower temporal integration window (step cycle) and a super-additive enhancement in a higher-order, broader temporal window (gait cycle).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about integration modes at different temporal scales.

claim: Neural responses at the lower-order timescale reflect a domain-general audiovisual integration process.
source: Furthermore, while neural responses at the lower-order timescale reflect a domain-general audiovisual integration process, cortical tracking at the higher-order timescale is exclusively engaged in the integration of biological motion cues.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this characterization of lower-order timescale responses.

claim: Cortical tracking at the higher-order timescale is exclusively engaged in the integration of biological motion cues.
source: Furthermore, while neural responses at the lower-order timescale reflect a domain-general audiovisual integration process, cortical tracking at the higher-order timescale is exclusively engaged in the integration of biological motion cues.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this characterization of higher-order timescale responses.

claim: Higher-order, domain-specific cortical tracking effect correlates with individuals' autistic traits.
source: In addition, only this higher-order, domain-specific cortical tracking effect correlates with individuals' autistic traits, highlighting its potential as a neural marker for autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this correlation finding.

claim: Humans can readily perceive biological motion from a visual display depicting just a handful of light dots attached to the head and major joints of a moving person.
source: Extensive evidence shows that humans can readily perceive BM from a visual display depicting just a handful of light dots attached to the head and major joints of a moving person (Blake and Shiffrar, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blake and Shiffrar, 2007.

claim: Integration of visual and auditory biological motion cues facilitates the detection, discrimination, and attentional processing of biological motion.
source: The integration of these visual and auditory BM cues facilitates the detection, discrimination, and attentional processing of BM (Mendonça et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2023a; Thomas and Shiffrar, 2013; van der Zwan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Multisensory benefits are diminished when visual biological motion is deprived of characteristic kinematic cues but not low-level motion attributes.
source: Notably, such benefits are diminished when the visual BM is deprived of characteristic kinematic cues but not low-level motion attributes (Brooks et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2023a; Thomas and Shiffrar, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Temporal windows of perceptual audiovisual synchrony are different between biological motion and non-biological motion stimuli.
source: and the temporal windows of perceptual audiovisual synchrony are different between BM and non-BM stimuli (Arrighi et al., 2006; Saygin et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arrighi et al., 2006 and Saygin et al., 2008.

claim: Integrating multisensory biological motion cues is foundational for perceiving and attending to other people and developing further social interaction.
source: In particular, integrating multisensory BM cues is foundational for perceiving and attending to other people and developing further social interaction.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the role of multisensory BM integration in social cognition.

claim: The ability to integrate multisensory biological motion cues is usually compromised in people with autism spectrum disorder.
source: Such ability is usually compromised in people with social deficits, such as individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (Falck-Ytter et al., 2013; Feldman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on ASD populations.

claim: Audiovisual integration of rhythmic stimuli may involve a process whereby brain activity aligns with and tracks external rhythms.
source: The audiovisual integration (AVI) of such rhythmic stimuli may involve a process whereby brain activity aligns with and tracks external rhythms, revealed by increased power or phase coherence of neural oscillations at corresponding frequencies (Bauer et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2016; Obleser and Kayser, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on cortical tracking.

claim: Temporal congruency in auditory and visual rhythms significantly enhances the cortical tracking of rhythmic stimulations in both modalities.
source: Studies based on simple or discrete stimuli show that temporal congruency in auditory and visual rhythms significantly enhances the cortical tracking of rhythmic stimulations in both modalities (Covic et al., 2017; Keitel and Müller, 2016; Nozaradan et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on simple rhythmic stimuli.

claim: Human locomotion movement has a narrower integration window consisting of each step (step cycle) and a broader integration window incorporating the opponent motion of the two feet (gait cycle).
source: For example, the human locomotion movement has a narrower integration window consisting of each step (i.e. step cycle) and a broader integration window incorporating the opponent motion of the two feet (i.e. gait cycle).
evidence: This is a description of the hierarchical structure of human locomotion.

claim: Neural tracking of nested kinematic structures contributes to the spatiotemporal integration of visual biological motion cues in different manners.
source: A recent study suggests that neural tracking of these nested kinematic structures contributes to the spatiotemporal integration of visual BM cues in different manners (Shen et al., 2023b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2023b.

claim: The additive model assumes independence between inputs from each sensory modality.
source: This model assumes independence between inputs from each sensory modality and distinguishes among sub-additive (AV<A +V), additive (AV = A +V), and super-additive (AV>A +V) response modes (see a review by Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the additive model framework, supported by a citation.

claim: The additive mode represents a linear combination between two modalities.
source: The additive mode represents a linear combination between two modalities.
evidence: This is a definition of the additive mode in multisensory integration.

claim: Super-additive mode indicates non-linear interaction processing with potentiated neural activation to facilitate the perception or detection of near-threshold signals.
source: In contrast, the super-additive and sub-additive modes indicate non-linear interaction processing, either with potentiated neural activation to facilitate the perception or detection of near-threshold signals (super-additive) or a deactivation mechanism to minimize the processing of redundant information cross-modally (sub-additive) (Laurienti et al., 2005; Metzger et al., 2020; Stanford et al., 2005; Wright et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on multisensory integration modes.

claim: Sub-additive mode indicates a deactivation mechanism to minimize the processing of redundant information cross-modally.
source: In contrast, the super-additive and sub-additive modes indicate non-linear interaction processing, either with potentiated neural activation to facilitate the perception or detection of near-threshold signals (super-additive) or a deactivation mechanism to minimize the processing of redundant information cross-modally (sub-additive) (Laurienti et al., 2005; Metzger et al., 2020; Stanford et al., 2005; Wright et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on multisensory integration modes.

claim: Inversion disrupts the unique, gravity-compatible kinematic features of biological motion but not the rhythmic signals generated by low-level motion cues.
source: Inversion disrupts the unique, gravity-compatible kinematic features of BM but not the rhythmic signals generated by low-level motion cues (Ma et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2023b; Simion et al., 2008; Troje and Westhoff, 2006; Wang et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on inversion effects.

claim: Individuals with varying social cognitive abilities lie on a continuum extending from clinical to nonclinical populations with different levels of autistic traits.
source: Since individuals with varying social cognitive abilities lie on a continuum extending from clinical to nonclinical populations with different levels of autistic traits, we investigated whether cortical tracking of audiovisual BM correlates with individuals' autistic traits, as measured by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about the continuum of autistic traits, with a citation to the AQ measure.

claim: Participants' performances for the color change detection task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 1a (mean accuracy>98%).
source: Behavioral analysis on all trials showed that their performances for the task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 1a (mean accuracy>98%; F (2, 46)=0.814, p=0.450, ƞp2=20.034)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: Participants' performances for the color change detection task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 1b (mean accuracy>98%).
source: Behavioral analysis on all trials showed that their performances for the task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 1a (mean accuracy>98%; F (2, 46)=0.814, p=0.450, ƞp2=20.034), Experiment 1b (mean accuracy>98%; F (2, 46)=0.615, p=0.545, ƞp2=20.026)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: Participants' performances for the color change detection task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 2 (mean accuracy>98%).
source: Behavioral analysis on all trials showed that their performances for the task were generally high and equally well in all conditions of Experiment 1a (mean accuracy>98%; F (2, 46)=0.814, p=0.450, ƞp2=20.034), Experiment 1b (mean accuracy>98%; F (2, 46)=0.615, p=0.545, ƞp2=20.026), and Experiment 2 (mean accuracy>98%; F (3, 69)=0.493, p=0.688, ƞp2=20.021)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: Comparable attention state was maintained across conditions in all experiments.
source: indicating comparable attention state across conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral performance data showing no differences across conditions.

claim: In Experiment 1a, the frequency of a full gait cycle is 1Hz, and the step-cycle frequency is 2Hz.
source: In Experiment 1a, the frequency of a full gait cycle is 1Hz, and the step-cycle frequency is 2Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: In Experiment 1a, responses in all three conditions (V, A, AV) showed clear peaks at step-cycle frequency (2Hz).
source: As shown in the grand average amplitude spectra (Figure 2a), both the responses in three conditions showed clear peaks at step-cycle frequency (2Hz; V: t (23)=6.963, p<0.001; A: t (23)=6.073, p<0.001; AV: t (23)=7.054, p<0.001; FDR corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG data and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: In Experiment 1a, only the response to audiovisual stimulation showed significant peaks at gait-cycle frequency (1Hz).
source: In contrast, at gait-cycle frequency (1Hz), only the response to AV stimulation showed significant peaks (V: t (23)=–2.072, p=0.975; A: t (23)=–0.054, p=0.521; AV: t (23)=4.059, p<0.001; FDR corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: In Experiment 1a, significant peaks were observed at 4Hz in all three conditions.
source: Besides, we also observed significant peaks at 4Hz in all three conditions (ps<0.001, FDR corrected), which showed a similar audiovisual integration mode as 2Hz (see more details in Appendix and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 1Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was greater than that in the visual condition.
source: At both 1Hz (Figure 2b) and 2Hz (Figure 2c), the amplitude in the AV condition was greater than that in the V condition (1Hz: t (23)=4.664, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.952; 2Hz: t (23)=5.132, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.048)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 2Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was greater than that in the visual condition.
source: At both 1Hz (Figure 2b) and 2Hz (Figure 2c), the amplitude in the AV condition was greater than that in the V condition (1Hz: t (23)=4.664, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.952; 2Hz: t (23)=5.132, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.048)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2c.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 1Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was greater than that in the auditory condition.
source: and the A condition (1Hz: t (23)=2.391, p=0.025, Cohen's d=0.488; 2Hz: t (23)=3.808, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.777), respectively, suggesting multisensory gains.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 2Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was greater than that in the auditory condition.
source: and the A condition (1Hz: t (23)=2.391, p=0.025, Cohen's d=0.488; 2Hz: t (23)=3.808, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.777), respectively, suggesting multisensory gains.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 1Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was significantly larger than the algebraic sum of those in the auditory and visual conditions, indicating super-additive audiovisual integration.
source: More importantly, at 1Hz, the amplitude in the AV condition was significantly larger than the algebraic sum of those in the A and V conditions (t (23)=3.028, p=0.006, Cohen's d=0.618), indicating a super-additive audiovisual integration effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing AV to A+V.

claim: In Experiment 1a, at 2Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was comparable to the unisensory sum, indicating additive audiovisual integration.
source: While at 2Hz, the amplitude in the AV condition was comparable to the unisensory sum (t (23)=–0.623, p=0.539, Cohen's d=–0.127), indicating additive audiovisual integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing AV to A+V.

claim: In Experiment 1b, the frequencies of the gait cycle and the corresponding step cycle were altered to 0.83Hz and 1.67Hz.
source: To further test whether such cortical tracking effect can apply to stimuli with a different speed, Experiment 1b altered the frequencies of the gait cycle and the corresponding step cycle to 0.83Hz and 1.67Hz while adopting the same paradigm as Experiment 1a.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1b, responses to V, A, and AV stimuli showed clear peaks at step-cycle frequency (1.67Hz).
source: As shown in Figure 2d, both the responses to V, A, and AV stimuli showed clear peaks at step-cycle frequency (1.67Hz; V: t (23)=3.473, p=0.001; A: t (23)=9.194, p<0.001; AV: t (23)=8.756, p<0.001; FDR corrected)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2d.

claim: In Experiment 1b, responses to V, A, and AV stimuli showed clear peaks at the harmonics of step-cycle frequency (3.33Hz).
source: and its harmonics (3.33Hz, ps<0.001, FDR corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at gait-cycle frequency (0.83Hz), only the response to audiovisual stimuli showed significant peaks.
source: In contrast, at gait-cycle frequency (0.83Hz), only the response to AV stimuli showed significant peaks (V: t (23)=–1.125, p=0.846; A: t (23)=–2.449, p=0.989; AV: t (23)=3.052, p=0.003; FDR corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 0.83Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the visual condition.
source: At both 0.83Hz (Figure 2e) and 1.67Hz (Figure 2f), the amplitude in the AV condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the V condition (0.83Hz: t (23)=2.665, p=0.014, Cohen's d=0.544; 1.67Hz: t (23)=6.380, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.302)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2e.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 1.67Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the visual condition.
source: At both 0.83Hz (Figure 2e) and 1.67Hz (Figure 2f), the amplitude in the AV condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the V condition (0.83Hz: t (23)=2.665, p=0.014, Cohen's d=0.544; 1.67Hz: t (23)=6.380, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.302)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2f.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 0.83Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the auditory condition.
source: and the A condition (0.83Hz: t (23)=3.625, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.740; 1.67Hz: t (23)=1.752, p=0.093, Cohen's d=0.358), respectively, suggesting multisensory gains.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 1.67Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was stronger or marginally stronger than that in the auditory condition.
source: and the A condition (0.83Hz: t (23)=3.625, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.740; 1.67Hz: t (23)=1.752, p=0.093, Cohen's d=0.358), respectively, suggesting multisensory gains.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 0.83Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was significantly larger than the sum of those in the auditory and visual conditions, indicating super-additive audiovisual integration.
source: More importantly, at 0.83Hz, the amplitude in the AV condition was significantly larger than the sum of those in the A and V conditions (t (23)=3.240, p=0.004, Cohen's d=0.661), indicating a super-additive audiovisual integration effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing AV to A+V.

claim: In Experiment 1b, at 1.67Hz, the amplitude in the audiovisual condition was comparable to the unisensory sum, indicating linear audiovisual integration.
source: By contrast, at 1.67Hz, the amplitude in the AV condition was comparable to the unisensory sum (t (23)=–0.735, p=0.470, Cohen's d=–0.150), indicating linear audiovisual integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing AV to A+V.

claim: In Experiment 1b, significant peaks were observed at 3.33Hz in all three conditions, which showed similar audiovisual integration mode as 1.67Hz.
source: Significant peaks were also observed at 3.33Hz in all three conditions (ps<0.001, FDR corrected), which showed similar audiovisual integration mode as 1.67Hz (see more details in Appendix and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Results from Experiments 1a and 1b consistently showed that the cortical tracking of the audiovisual signals at different temporal scales exhibit distinct audiovisual integration modes.
source: In summary, results from Experiments 1a and 1b consistently showed that the cortical tracking of the audiovisual signals at different temporal scales exhibit distinct audiovisual integration modes, i.e., the super-additive effect at gait-cycle frequency and the additive effect at step-cycle frequency
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings from Experiments 1a and 1b.

claim: The cortical tracking effects at the two temporal scales might be driven by functionally dissociable mechanisms.
source: indicating that the cortical tracking effects at the two temporal scales might be driven by functionally dissociable mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the different integration modes observed at different temporal scales.

claim: In Experiment 2, the task and the frequencies of visual stimuli were the same as Experiment 1a.
source: The task and the frequencies of visual stimuli in Experiment 2 were same as Experiment 1a.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The audiovisual congruency effect can be taken as an index of audiovisual integration.
source: The audiovisual congruency effect, characterized by stronger neural responses in the audiovisual congruent condition compared with the incongruent condition, can be taken as an index of AVI (Fleming et al., 2020; Maddox et al., 2015; Wuerger et al., 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on audiovisual congruency effects.

claim: A stronger congruency effect in the upright condition relative to the inverted condition characterizes an audiovisual integration process specific to biological motion information.
source: A stronger congruency effect in the upright condition relative to the inverted condition characterizes an AVI process specific to BM information.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would indicate BM-specific processing.

claim: In Experiment 2, at 1Hz, the congruency effect in the upright condition was significantly stronger than that in the inverted condition in a cluster at the right hemisphere.
source: At 1Hz, the congruency effect in the upright condition was significantly stronger than that in the inverted condition in a cluster at the right hemisphere (Figure 3a, lower panel, p=0.029; C2, CPz, CP2, CP4, CP6, Pz, P2, P4, P6).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation test and reference to Figure 3a.

claim: In Experiment 2, audiovisual congruency enhanced the oscillatory amplitude only for upright biological motion but not when visual biological motion was inverted at 1Hz.
source: Results showed that (Figure 3b) audiovisual congruency enhanced the oscillatory amplitude only for upright BM (t (23)=4.632, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.945) but not when visual BM was inverted (t (23)=0.480, p=0.635, Cohen's d=0.098).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3b.

claim: Cortical tracking of the high-order gait cycles involves a domain-specific process exclusively engaged in the audiovisual integration of biological motion.
source: Together, these findings suggest that cortical tracking of the high-order gait cycles involves a domain-specific process exclusively engaged in the AVI of BM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inversion effect observed at gait-cycle frequency.

claim: In Experiment 2, at 2Hz, no cluster showed a significantly different congruency effect between the upright and inverted conditions.
source: In contrast, at 2Hz, no cluster showed a significantly different congruency effect between the upright and inverted conditions (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation test and reference to Figure 3d.

claim: In Experiment 2, both upright and inverted stimuli induced a significant congruency effect at 2Hz.
source: Results showed that both upright and inverted stimuli induced a significant congruency effect at 2Hz (Figure 3e; upright: t (23)=3.096, p=0.005, Cohen's d=0.632; inverted: t (23)=2.672, p=0.014, Cohen's d=0.545).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3e.

claim: Neural tracking of the lower-order step cycles is associated with a domain-general audiovisual integration process mostly driven by temporal correspondence in physical stimuli.
source: These findings suggest that neural tracking of the lower-order step cycles is associated with a domain-general AVI process mostly driven by temporal correspondence in physical stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of inversion effect at step-cycle frequency.

claim: There is a negative correlation between individuals' AQ scores and their neural responses at 1Hz (r=–0.493, p=0.017).
source: After removing one outlier (whose neural response exceeded 3 SD from the group mean), we observed an evident negative correlation between individuals' AQ scores and their neural responses at 1Hz (Figure 3c, r=–0.493, p=0.017)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3c.

claim: There is no significant correlation between individuals' AQ scores and their neural responses at 2Hz (r=–0.158, p=0.460).
source: but not at 2Hz (Figure 3f, r=–0.158, p=0.460).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3f.

claim: The lack of significant correlation results at 2Hz was not attributable to electrode selection bias based on the significant cluster at 1Hz.
source: The lack of significant results at 2Hz was not attributable to electrode selection bias based on the significant cluster at 1Hz, as similar results were observed when we performed analyses on clusters showing non-selective significant congruency effects at 2Hz (see the control analysis in Appendix and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analyses described in the appendix.

claim: Compared with the high AQ group, the low AQ group showed a greater BM-specific cortical tracking effect at 1Hz but not at 2Hz.
source: Besides, we split the participants based on their median AQ score and found that, compared with the high AQ group, the low AQ group showed a greater BM-specific cortical tracking effect at 1Hz but not at 2Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by group comparison analysis described in the appendix.

claim: Observers' neural activity tracked the temporally corresponding audiovisual biological motion signals at the frequencies of two rhythmic structures under a motion-irrelevant color detection task.
source: We found that, even under a motion-irrelevant color detection task, observers' neural activity tracked the temporally corresponding audiovisual BM signals at the frequencies of two rhythmic structures, i.e., the higher-order structure of gait cycle at a larger integration window and the basic-level structure of step cycle at a smaller integration window.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: The strength of cortical tracking effects was enhanced under the audiovisual condition than in the visual-only or auditory-only condition, indicating multisensory gains.
source: The strength of these cortical tracking effects was enhanced under the audiovisual condition than in the visual-only or auditory-only condition, indicating multisensory gains.
evidence: This is a summary of the multisensory enhancement findings.

claim: At step-cycle frequency, the cortical tracking effect in the audiovisual condition equaled the additive sum of the unisensory conditions.
source: At step-cycle frequency, the cortical tracking effect in the AV condition equaled the additive sum of the unisensory conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the additive integration finding at step-cycle frequency.

claim: Linear integration at step-cycle frequency may result from concurrent, independent processing of unisensory inputs without additional interaction of them.
source: Such linear integration may result from concurrent, independent processing of unisensory inputs without additional interaction of them (Stein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the additive integration mode, supported by a citation.

claim: At gait-cycle frequency, the congruent audiovisual signals led to a super-additive multisensory enhancement over the linear combination of auditory and visual conditions.
source: In contrast, at gait-cycle frequency, the congruent audiovisual signals led to a super-additive multisensory enhancement over the linear combination of auditory and visual conditions (AV>A +V)
evidence: This is a summary of the super-additive integration finding at gait-cycle frequency.

claim: There was no evident cortical tracking effect in the visual condition at gait-cycle frequency, different from previous findings obtained with a motion-relevant change detection task.
source: despite that there was no evident cortical tracking effect in the visual condition, different from previous findings obtained with a motion-relevant change detection task (Shen et al., 2023b).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Super-additive multisensory enhancement may bring about decreased thresholds of detection and identification.
source: This super-additive multisensory enhancement may bring about decreased thresholds of detection and identification (Stanford et al., 2005)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of super-additive enhancement, supported by a citation.

claim: Super-additive multisensory enhancement allows people to achieve a more clear and stable perception of the external environment and detect weak stimulus changes in time and respond adaptively.
source: allowing people to achieve a more clear and stable perception of the external environment and detect weak stimulus changes in time and respond adaptively.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional benefits of super-additive enhancement.

claim: The audiovisual integration effect at step-cycle frequency was significant for both upright and inverted biological motion signals and comparable between the two conditions.
source: In particular, the AVI effect at step-cycle frequency was significant for both upright and inverted BM signals and comparable between the two conditions
evidence: This is a summary of the findings at step-cycle frequency in Experiment 2.

claim: The audiovisual integration effect at gait-cycle frequency was only significant in the upright condition and was greater than that in the inverted condition.
source: while the AVI effect at gait-cycle frequency was only significant in the upright condition and was greater than that in the inverted condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings at gait-cycle frequency in Experiment 2.

claim: The inversion effect has long been regarded as a marker of the specificity of biological motion processing in numerous behavioral and neuroimaging studies.
source: The inversion effect has long been regarded as a marker of the specificity of BM processing in numerous behavioral and neuroimaging studies (Grossman and Blake, 2001; Ma et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2023b; Simion et al., 2008; Troje and Westhoff, 2006; Vallortigara and Regolin, 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Wang and Jiang, 2012; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on inversion effects.

claim: The neural encoding of the higher-order rhythmic structure reflects the audiovisual integration of biological motion and contributes to the specialized processing of biological motion information.
source: Our current findings of the inversion effect in the cortical tracking of audiovisual BM at the gait-cycle frequency suggest that the neural encoding of the higher-order rhythmic structure reflects the AVI of BM and contributes to the specialized processing of BM information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inversion effect observed at gait-cycle frequency.

claim: The cortical tracking of the step cycle may reflect the integration of basic motion signals and corresponding sounds.
source: In contrast, the cortical tracking of the step cycle may reflect the integration of basic motion signals and corresponding sounds.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of step-cycle tracking.

claim: The neural tracking of rhythmic structures at different temporal scales plays distinct roles in the audiovisual integration of biological motion, which may result from the interplay of stimulus-driven and domain-specific mechanisms.
source: Together, these results reveal that the neural tracking of rhythmic structures at different temporal scales plays distinct roles in the AVI of BM, which may result from the interplay of stimulus-driven and domain-specific mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary inference about the mechanisms underlying the findings.

claim: The BM-specific audiovisual integration effect was associated with neural activity in the right temporoparietal electrodes.
source: Besides the temporal dynamics of neural activity revealed by the cortical tracking process, we found that the BM-specific AVI effect was associated with neural activity in the right temporoparietal electrodes.
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of the BM-specific effect.

claim: The right temporoparietal finding likely relates to the activation of the right posterior superior temporal sulcus, a region responding to both auditory and visual biological motion information and being causally involved in biological motion perception.
